commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether documenting a tool-specific monitoring plan before go-live reduces undetected harm or performance degradation, and no study documents the hazard itself. Sixteen sources endorse the practice, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and regulatory expectation rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The sixteen endorsements agree that monitoring should occur, but agreement among guidance documents is a form of expert opinion. It does not show that a written plan changes detection rates or patient outcomes.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions lists ongoing performance monitoring as a lifecycle expectation. The CDRH discussion paper on generative AI devices asks whether machine-based supervisory agents could support postmarket monitoring and how those agents would themselves be evaluated. These documents signal regulatory direction, though neither states a documented local plan requirement for health systems.

FAIR-AI requires a monitoring plan for every deployed tool, maintained through periodic attestation by a named business owner. The RUAIH guidance similarly asks organizations to identify responsible parties. The supplied sources give no data on staff hours, cost, or the number of tools a governance group can monitor, so the burden at scale remains unmeasured.

The radiology multi-society statement leaves the definition of sufficient monitoring to local oversight groups on a case-by-case basis, and the NASEM-style delivery guidance stresses baseline data architecture. This suggests that plan content will vary widely across tools and sites. No supplied study reports whether such plans are completed, followed, or kept current after go-live.

The HEAAL framework asks developers and deployers to devise strategies for ongoing monitoring, feedback, and evaluation across the lifecycle. No supplied study examines whether monitoring plans include subgroup performance measures or whether they detect degradation that falls unevenly on particular patient groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare tools deployed with and without a documented, owner-assigned monitoring plan and measure time to detection of performance drift or safety events, the frequency of plan adherence after go-live, and the staffing cost of maintaining plans across a tool portfolio.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence on whether monitoring plans detect harms specific to them, and safety-net sites may have less data infrastructure to carry out the plans these sources describe.
